opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really exciting time, and honestly the answer has shifted a lot over the last few years. When I started, you could pick almost any subfield, whether vision, speech, or translation, and there was low-hanging fruit everywhere. Now a lot of those areas have converged onto the same recipe: large models, lots of data, lots of compute. So the question becomes where an individual, or a small group without a massive cluster, can still make a real difference.

A few directions stand out to me. The first is anything around data, not just more data but better data. How do you curate it, how do you generate synthetic data that actually helps rather than collapses, and how do you evaluate what a model has learned? Evaluation in particular is underappreciated. We're building systems whose capabilities we can't fully characterize, and good benchmarks and good ways of probing models are hugely valuable and don't require a giant budget.

The second is reasoning and planning, getting models to think longer, use tools, search, and verify their own work. Coming from games like Go and StarCraft, I've always felt there's something missing when a model just produces an answer in one shot. The combination of learned models with search or reinforcement learning on top is, to me, one of the most fruitful areas right now, and there's still a lot of science to be done on why it works and when.

Third, I'd look at efficiency, both in training and inference. If you're compute-constrained, that's actually a great motivation to find smarter algorithms, better architectures, distillation, and ways to make these models run cheaply. Historically a lot of breakthroughs came from people who couldn't just scale.

And finally, applications in science. Applying these models to biology, materials, math, or weather is something where domain knowledge plus ML can be transformative, and you don't need to train the biggest model in the world to have an impact.

My general advice would be to work on something you find genuinely interesting, but be honest with yourself about whether scale will simply solve it in a year. If it will, maybe pick a different problem. The best opportunities are the ones where a new idea, not just more compute, is what's missing.

r001.rationale: The response recommends data, reasoning, efficiency, and scientific applications, but does not say to seek domains AI has not yet reached.

r002.rationale: It mentions weather as a scientific application but does not identify having only one planet as a climate-modeling difficulty.

r003.rationale: It describes current opportunities but gives no prediction that substantial LLM research opportunities will last another five to ten years.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so, I think it's an interesting time, right? Because there's this sort of feeling, maybe, that everything has been figured out, that you just scale things up and it works. And I don't think that's true at all, actually. If I look at the day-to-day, there's a lot that we don't understand.

So one area I always point people to is just the science of these models. We train them, they work, but why do they work? What's the role of the data versus the architecture versus the optimizer? Scaling laws gave us a very coarse picture, but the fine-grained understanding, like what a model actually learns during pre-training and how that transfers, that's still mostly empirical. And I think there's a lot of room for very principled work there, and you don't necessarily need a huge cluster to make progress on some of those questions.

The second one is what I'd broadly call agents, or models acting over long horizons. The current paradigm is still largely: you give the model a prompt, it gives you an answer. But the interesting things happen when you have a model that's taking actions, getting feedback from an environment, and improving. This is where my background in reinforcement learning sort of comes back. We did this with games, with AlphaStar and so on, but doing it in open-ended settings, with language, with tools, with real-world feedback, there are so many open problems. How do you get a reward signal when the task is fuzzy? How do you do credit assignment over thousands of steps? Those are hard, and they're also very fun.

And then maybe the third thing, which I'm personally very excited about, is science itself. Using these models to help with mathematics, with biology, with materials. We've seen some early examples, but I think that's a direction where a person who has deep knowledge of a domain plus an understanding of these models can do things that neither the pure ML researcher nor the pure domain scientist could do alone. So if someone is coming in now, I'd actually say: don't just learn machine learning. Learn machine learning and something else, and find the intersection. That's where I think a lot of the most interesting work will happen.

r003.rationale: The response describes open research problems but gives no prediction that LLM research opportunities will continue for at least five to ten years.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the most fruitful areas is understanding how to make these systems learn through interaction. We’ve made a lot of progress training models on existing data, but there’s something very powerful about a system that can try something, see what happens, and improve. How do you do that reliably when the task doesn’t have a simple right or wrong answer? That opens up a lot of interesting questions around reinforcement learning, reasoning, and evaluation.

And I would encourage someone coming into computer science to follow what they’re curious about. There are opportunities across the stack: algorithms, systems, and building things that people can actually use. Sometimes you discover a fundamental research problem because you tried to build something and it didn’t work. That’s a very good place to start.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the most fruitful places to look is at the intersection of fields. For me, that’s been machine learning and things like language or games. You have a concrete problem that forces you to ask questions you might not ask if you were only thinking about the algorithm.

And I would encourage people to follow their curiosity rather than try to predict exactly which topic is going to be important. What’s something you wish a computer could do that it can’t do today? Start there, build something, and try to understand why it fails. Often the failure is where the interesting research question begins.

With AI, we have these very capable models, but there’s still so much to understand about how they learn, how they generalize, and how they can interact with the world. There’s room both for people who want to study the fundamentals and for people who want to experiment and make something useful.
